title: Can a movie be a movie without being "storytellling"?

commenti.body: [removed]

I mean there are definitely experimental pieces of film that do not consist of any sense of storytelling. I think where it gets interesting is that because humans love seeing stories in stuff, a viewer watching could probably construct a story out of a bunch of nonsensical moving pictures(not all will, maybe the vast majority won't, but some will). 

It also depends on a couple things, like if a movie inadvertently can be constructed into a story in someone's mind even though that was not the intention of the filmmaker, does the movie still have storytelling baked into it by accident? 

But I don't think movies are defined as anything more than motion pictures, so movies aren't bounded by storytelling. I think in my brain, though, storytelling has the potential to be almost boundless.

I have two clarifying questions for you.

1. What is your definition of storytelling here? I think the discussion is going to hinge around this. If a story is just a chronological series of events or images of any type, then it would be very hard indeed to find a story-less film.
2. Are you including avant-garde films/video art in this discussion, in addition to mainstream feature films? If so, I think it is possible to find a movie with little to no storytelling.

A few examples:

[OM directed by John Smith](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YobqR-RTFLM) could be interpreted as having a story. There is an event, it happens, it ends. But the main focus of this short film is an audiovisual pun. Would you consider this film as storytelling?

[Black Ice by Stan Brakhage](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5VXOYYXBCck): Would you consider this film to be storytelling? I suppose one could interpret it as an abstract representation of a voyage through space.

[Dots by Norman McLaren](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E3-vsKwQ0Cg&list=PLpHLBf41xLlCugybuoZmiXUyq8nJiMKlk&index=1): Does a series of audiovisual events that happen one after another count as a story? A film like this lacks many of the vital aspects of storytelling, like characters who have goals and face conflicts in achieving those goals.

To you, do any of these three films count as non-storytelling?

Yes, there's been plenty of movies, most of them short films, that have been "movies" without telling a story. The example that immediately comes to mind for me is Wavelength, an experimental film that is just a shot of a wall, and over the course of the movie the camera gradually moves towards the wall. Stuff does happen, someone walks into frame and dies, someone walks into frame later and makes a phone call, presumably to 911, but there's no traditional narrative to speak of. If there is one, it's one that's projected by the audience. Another one is Empire, Andy Warhol's 9 hour long movie that is just a shot of the empire state building, through which we see lights turn on and off, the background change, and many other minor variations. Again, any story is projected by the audience. Yet another example is Un Chien Andalou, the first and most famous experimental film. Despite there being something resembling a narrative, directors Luis Buńuel and Salvador Dali insisted that the movie has absolutely no meaning, and that it can, at best, be read on a psychological level because every moment was thought into being at pure randomness.

I could go on but you get my gist. In experimental movies narrative is regularly abandoned for some other methods, and even in more mainstream movies like Fantasia, they can run the gambit from straightforward stories to near complete abstraction. So yes, ots possible for movies to not tell stories.

Can a poem be a poem without telling a story? In Aristotle’s time this would be an absurd gesture, as poets and ‘storytellers’ were one and the same. Poems were innately the base for which tragedies, comedies, and historic narratives were played out. Then slowly over the western canon poetry got more specific, and in the modern tradition more abstract. Now we can clearly delineate between poetry that tells a narrative, and that which uses the form to evoke pure, lyrical feeling. I understand the question though. Since cinéma has to inherently show something material in order to be, (rather than an amalgamation of symbols we’ve inscribed value and meaning in) is it possible for it to be abstracted, since it’s always ‘real’? Even experimental films which aren’t filming anything, and consist totally of scratch marks made by the artist directly on the celluloid are still a document of that material process. That’s not a story being imagined or projected by the viewer, that is simply what is being shown. I think that like with poetry, (and all mediums) over time cinema will become fractured in its conventions. As of now, computer generated (not referring to AI generated, which is neither photography nor cinema) filmmaking has generally adhered to the norms of traditional narrative modes, but I could see there being a break where we see forms of ‘filmmaking’ produced entirely digitally which have no basis in material reality, and thus no fabric for us to form a story out of. (If anyone has any examples of this which exist already, I’d love to know about it.)

John Whitney (probably best known for the abstract *Vertigo* credits sequence) was a pioneering computer animator.  
Would you say any of his computer graphics films county as legitimate non-stories?

[Matrix III](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZrKgyY5aDvA)

[Arabesque](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cxkbScwt77g)

Your question is very interesting but I think is based on premises more relevant to marketing or cataloguing than actual categories that are coherent within the art of cinema.

\> If moving pictures can qualify as a movie without any element of storytelling. 

There are three nouns here: "moving pictures" is clear enough, but what is "a movie" if not just a synonym of that? In which case by definition, moving pictures makes a movie. 

Finally "storytelling". How much narrative or dialogue-driven recounting of a story is needed to qualify here? Dicussion of the Kuleshov effect and editing montage seems to show that we are ready to build a story out of images no matter what.

Take for example Kubrick's 2001: the first parts are clear enough as a narrative but in the last 30 minutes the narrative breaks down completely. We are ready to build a story from the abstract images Kubrick gives us, but is that a narrative or something we just imagined?

When you get to talking about mainstream commercial film vs more artistic and experimental film, this is where the question makes sense. And it's fundamentally a marketing question. 

In this case "a movie" is something that the general public might pay to see and historically there are very few films that can do that without a recognisable narrative. But Koyonasqaatsi has done quite well over the years, and there are a few more like that. Under the Skin is quite light on story and did quite well. So it can be done within limits.  

Here is my list of abstract films that have no recognisable narrative:

[https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/list/abstract/](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/list/abstract/)

>Take for example Kubrick's 2001: the first parts are clear enough as a narrative but in the last 30 minutes the narrative breaks down completely. We are ready to build a story from the abstract images Kubrick gives us, but is that a narrative or something we just imagined?

I feel like there is a definite narrative here within the abstraction. The novel makes it fairly explicit. >!David Bowman traveling through the wormhole and then becoming uplifted by the aliens into the next step of human evolution, continuing the process that began at the very beginning of the film.!<

I don’t know that “showing something material” is any more “storytelling” than abstract poetry, myself.

It’s also certainly not true that cinema has “generally adhered to the norms of traditional narrative modes”, it’s just easier to find that type because it is popular. Same in writing. Poetry itself is a small niche of writing, and abstract poetry a niche of a niche.

Films that tell a story are called 'narrative cinema'.  I think your puzzlement comes from your equating moving pictures which show 'something happening' (some sort of change in a series of images of people, places, things over time) with 'telling a story'.  But change isn't adequate for narrative.  There are thousands of films in existence that document 'something happening' but don't have anything resembling a story - Andy Warhol's **Empire** (USA, 1965) is an example (it is available on YouTube if you have a spare 8 hours).

A story is told via film when a series of images & sounds are structured by a plot and the events portrayed onscreen have a causal connection involving the key characters over time.  Generally, it is accepted that the actions portrayed must arise from some sort of conflict (man vs society, man vs nature, present security undermined by past actions, etc.)  Of course, there must be a sense of unity to the imagery and film techniques are available to create this (choices of certain dominant colors, sounds, music, type of dialogue, etc.)

Most people associate narrative cinema with movies that have strong, relatable character types, lots of physical action or verbal pyrotechnics, and a plot that advances steadily toward a climax (and then the film ends).  But so-called 'art house films' are also narrative films.  Many people find them boring to watch, since such films are often less plot-driven than Hollywood movies and the people who make them are satisfied with a level of ambiguity (in the character's behavior) and a complexity of tone and atmosphere that are rarely found in mass entertainment.

How definite is it really though? Just judging from the images presented in the film, and not from the extraneous info we might have from outside? It's a tricky question for me because I read the Clarke novel way before I saw the film, so I try to deprogram myself from the narrative I learned as a very young kid.

I can honestly say that I saw the film for the first time at age 10 or so, well before I read the book, and that's how I read it. I think that, even without that extra context, there is enough of a parallel with the opening sequence to at least suggest that narrative.

In a post above I linked to the [John Smith film OM](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YobqR-RTFLM) which does arguably tell a  very simple story: a >!man sits down at a barber shop, the barber shaves his head, the barber finishes the haircut and takes off his customer's bib.!<

Does a narrative of logically connected events count as a story? Obviously, that's not the point of this film, which is about creating an audiovisual pun that surprises the viewer.

Fair enough, I'll accept that. 

Anyhow, I think we can agree that 2001 is pushing the envelope as far as a mainstream film breaking up explicit narrative in favour of abstraction. Much more than that and it would cease to be acceptable for commercial audiences - and would probably be unacceptable to multiplex audiences today, I would imagine.

Would you agree that any of the art film/video art examples I've posted elsewhere in this thread count as genuinely storyless? Or is a sheer series of consecutive visual events enough to create a story in the viewer's imagination?
I guess that depends on how you define "cinema." I mean, both Ron Howard and Nam Jun Paik make motion pictures, but clearly there's a tremendous aesthetic gap between them.

We’re not really talking about preferences or quality, just form. And if we’re talking about the theoretical formal potentials of movies, I don’t think we need to confine ourselves to talking about Ron Howard.

I did not mean that post to be a commentary on preferences or quality and just used Ron Howard's name as kind of a synecdoche for mainstream Hollywood cinema.

Let me try to clarify.

"Cinema" encompasses a tremendous range of aesthetic goals and experiences. I'm agreeing with your statement that 

>It’s also certainly not true that cinema has “generally adhered to the norms of traditional narrative modes”, it’s just easier to find that type because it is popular. 

by pointing out just how aesthetically different two filmmakers can be and still conceivably both be called filmmakers. We can identify many other cases of films or filmmakers that fall under the same medium while being about as aesthetically different as it's possible to be. *La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon* and *Toy Story 3* are very different viewer experiences and were produced in very different ways but still both fall into the category of 'cinema.'

I feel that the Dadaists and surrealists explored this question. Un chien andalous for example can hardly be called storytelling, it destroys any attempt of finding a narrative. But it seems very conscious of how hard it is to accomplish that and that the viewer will constantly attempt to find a narrative.

You can go much more stark than that.

Look in your cell phone. You are a filmmaker. That time you accidentally hit record? Movie. That time you filmed your dog at the dog park because you thought she would play with the other dog but didn’t? Movie.

In the distant past you were more likely to find a movie in the hands of people that paid a lot of money. That changed a long time ago with home video cameras. If we look into the small niche of movies that were produced to be shown to strangers, then money gets involved and everything goes downhill. Filmmaking can incredibly expensive and time consuming, and most people genuinely don’t have much interest in non-storytelling based movies. Music has a bit more room for poetry, but is still dominated by singers. And bad poetry. Even dancers talk about “storytelling”, it’s wild. But there is certainly potential for other possibilities - music, sure, but even something as a podcast of people sharing knowledge or improvising or talking without an underlying story are wildly popular. And sometimes they have stories, or resort to storytelling - but not always.

More possibilities exist.

The underlying question that isn’t asked here that always exists in every conversation that someway relates to commercial cinema: Will anyone pay to market these other options to me? The answer is no, you have to find or make it yourself, and that in itself is why we live in a world where it is even possible for someone to ask a question like this in the first place. Stories make more money. If your interests lie beyond that, in this world, the cost to explore is on you.

I haven't seen those ones before this, notice they're not on my "abstract" playlist, so I can't say right now. But I'll take a look at them and get back to you. 

Without prejudicing the eventual answer I would tentatively say yes, pretty much any conjunction of images in sequence can have that effect.

Nomadland is famously a film about nothing. You keep waiting and waiting and thinking the story is about to start. But no. A seasonal Amazon worker likes van life and drives around. The Oscar awards loved it. But I was taught as a child that a story had a plot that crescendos to the climax, then a short decrescendo to the end. I guess Nomadland tells an excruciatingly boring story. Warehouse worker drives around, she stops and talks to a guy, then drives around more. I wouldn’t be angry if I heard someone argue that it’s a film about nothing and that it’s not high art, it’s a film with no story, but still a film.

>Andy Warhol's Empire (USA, 1965) is an example (it is available on YouTube if you have a spare 8 hours).

just to note, i am pretty sure every copy floating out there is a recreation (from 2012, by Eric Doeringer) and not the actual movie itself, how much that distinction actually matters is debatable.

Not that it's the easiest thing to descipher if you have ONLY watched the film. But, yes, above poster is absolutely correct on that front. Clarke envisioned a story heavily borrowing from Nietzschean philosophy. Right down to the opening theme song, Thus Spoke Zarathustra. 

In that book, Nietzsche blends most of his past philosophical ideas and projects into a single biblical-like tale. One of Nietzsche's concepts in that book, if taken literally, is the idea of an Overman, or artistically interpreted as the next stage of evolution that we are to reach for. Beast on one end at the morning of our evolution, midday as represented by our current state and night as some future state that we cannot reach and representitive of transformation. 

The film is heavily exploring the concept of passive nihilism turning into active nihilism by a sort of self-overcoming, self affirmation and choice. David Bowman starts down this path by actively choosing his own self interest over the AI computer that unitl now he's entrusted himself and the mission to. The Alien entity advances David to the next stage of evolution only because he has taken this step. 

The film I think in part is ultimately exploring the idea of challenging culture, the status quo, whatever we've blindly been following, and by taking that step of moving away from passivity we move forward and advance as a species.

I think your interpretation is very interesting, and I would only take issue with the very definiteness you employ. To say that one idea or other about this highly ambiguous film is "absolutely correct" is to impose a clarity on it that is deliberately subtracted by Kubrick.

I agree that the film is exploring issues of nihilism, even the Nietzchean Death of God, and self-overcoming. However, suggesting the film follows Zarathustra thematically would be going a step too far IMO. 

Because if God is Dead as per Nietzsche, the mysterious alien entities seem to replace it. So mankind's self-evolution as figured in Zarathustra is replaced here by a forced evolution carried out by aliens/monolith on the passive Bowman.

I know that the aliens have a metaphorical function and don't "really exist" in this reading, or exist only as symbols of human self-striving, but you get my drift, that the ambiguity of 2001 as a philosophical text precludes the kind of definite reading you prefer.

I took up your challenge and looked at these films so here's my answer:

OM is a joke, "OM to OI!", that is witty enough to provoke a passing smile but not much more. Insofar as it is a joke it's a narrative, as jokes are often little stories. I will definitely steal it for a music vid though. 

Black Ice is as purely abstract as it gets. Not a story at all, despite the sense of travelling into the space. 0% narrative content. Seriously boring despite lasting only 2 minutes. Which is why Dog Star Man is better, it has something you can hang your narrative hat on. 

Dots was too annoying to follow for more than 10 seconds. Pass on judgement here. 

Conclusion: it is indeed possible to create visual moving pictures with no narrative at all, but you have to try hard to be abstract like Brakhage.

This sums up my thoughts rather well and I even had the same examples in mind (at least Dots). I would say any divergence a filmmaker makes from the black screen is an act of storytelling as it entails the narrative position that there is something, rather than nothing. 

The most basic thing you could do by that logic would be Kubelka's [Arnulf Rainer (1960)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vfy1cdRrAFU) which is so basic that he could convert it into [a wall instalation](https://farm9.staticflickr.com/8069/8213466591_813a301345_z.jpg) that looks like a normal painting (but really it's the frame-sequence from the film). 

Of course with a more conservative definition of storytelling that demands for instance a story must have characters, this would probably not fly.
thoughts on my favorite film, Stranger Than Paradise? :)
[removed]
Very useful information, thank you.

Yes I think you've got that right. This is simply a take from Clarke / Kubrick employing a few obvious Nietzchean themes. 

For Neitzche, the Overman was something to aspire to, not actually become, in the same way it would be impossible to transform ourselves through evolutionary means in just a lifetime. 

The concept of the Overman does in essence, replace God, replace Christianity. It provides something for us to "reach for" in the way religion does induce a sort of lifestyle of overcoming in its own particular way. So I think you could definitely replace God with this alien entity and that is a valid take too. 

I think there are many ways you can interpret the metaphors in 2001, it is fun to look at it through a Nietzsche-lens because it works almost too well. But yes, nailing down the images of 2001 into a specific Nietzsche shaped box does take out a lot of mystery and personal interepretation out of it, which I think Kubrick would probably be against

Definitely agree that this is a fun way of looking atb how the film develops, and will definitely take it for a spin next time I check out the film... seems that might be overdue before the end of the year. Cheers
I think it absolutely has a story and characters with motivations.
I guess I'm just more interested in/open to film as a purely audiovisual experience.

Wasn't the point of the exercise not whether we like it or not but whether it actually can generate some kind of narrative from minimal input?

I would say it's the "audio" part of audiovisual here that was failing for me. 

Black Ice has no audio at all which makes it just an abstract moving image. Why couldn't Brakhage put some kind of soundtrack on it?

And it's the annoying "bloop bloop" sound that drove me away from Dots right away.

I think there are directors already experimenting with this, not writing scripts but rather describing images, improvising etc. But I think combining multiple images together, or even composing or lighting is storytelling already. If you compose left or right, if there is more space at the bottom or top. If the image is contrasty or flat, sidelit, backlit, frontlit... I think movies without storytelling would be just bad movies. Or even - bad photographs, passport or catalogue photos. But even that would ask questions. "Why is someone presenting me an informational image and telling me to watch it? There must be a backstory to this..."

As I read your opening post, I said to myself.. "there is a story everywhere" .. so, IMO, showing a series of moving pictures also has a story to say.. :)

As "there is a story everywhere".. movies are more about *how* they say or show the story, more than the story itself.. atleast for me, personally.
